claims.text: Low-temperature synthesis can inhibit precursor mobility during HEA nanoparticle formation.
Inhibiting precursor mobility favors formation of a single-phase HEA nanoparticle.
Low-temperature solvothermal synthesis reliably produces single-phase PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles.
Restricted precursor mobility prevents agglomeration of noble metals.
Restricted precursor mobility enforces a random, isolated distribution of Pt and Pd within PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles.
Alloying Co, Cu, and Ni with Pt and Pd can produce isolated Pt and Pd sites.
PtPdCoCuNi alloying produces charge transfer to Pt and Pd species.
The transferred charge specifically originates from adjacent inexpensive transition-metal atoms.
Ligand and electronic effects in HEAs modify the electronic properties of active sites.
A random distribution of isolated Pt and Pd maximizes ligand and electronic cocktail effects.
Charge transfer to isolated Pt and Pd sites strengthens interaction with nitrobenzene and enhances hydrogenation activity.
PtPdCoCuNi/SiO2 has higher aniline yield in nitrobenzene hydrogenation than PtPd/SiO2.
A low-temperature PtPdCoCuNi catalyst will contain more isolated Pt/Pd sites than an otherwise comparable high-temperature catalyst.
A low-temperature PtPdCoCuNi catalyst will show greater charge transfer and higher nitrobenzene-hydrogenation performance than a high-temperature control.
Conventional high-temperature synthesis tends to produce aggregated noble-metal clusters with weaker charge transfer and lower catalytic activity.
The proposed mechanism may cease to hold when solvent, precursor ratios, or metal combinations differ substantially.

contradictions.description: The top-level hypothesis describes enhanced charge transfer as the route by which isolated Pt/Pd sites form, whereas the mechanism says restricted mobility first creates isolated Pt/Pd sites and that this distribution then promotes charge transfer, reversing the causal ordering.
